plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a labeled cross-sectional diagram of a Downs cell, the industrial electrolytic apparatus used to produce pure sodium metal from molten sodium chloride via the reaction 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g). The cell interior contains a bath of molten NaCl, with a cylindrical iron screen separating the electrode compartments; the cathode (−) occupies the outer annular region and the anode (+) projects upward from the bottom center, both connected to an external voltage source at the lower right. Liquid sodium metal, which is less dense than the molten salt, rises and collects in a side reservoir on the right, from which it drains through a labeled Na outlet; simultaneously, Cl2 gas produced at the anode rises through a central green-tinted collector tube and exits through a labeled Cl2 outlet at the upper right, while fresh NaCl is fed continuously through an inlet at the top. The iron screen physically segregates the two products — liquid sodium and gaseous chlorine — preventing their recombination and enabling continuous, separate collection of each. This figure demonstrates the Downs cell as the industrial-scale process for sodium production and explains why aqueous electrolysis cannot substitute for it, since H+ ions are more easily reduced than Na+ ions at any cathode in contact with water.

interactionPlan.concept: A Downs cell electrolyzes molten NaCl into liquid sodium at the outer cathode and chlorine gas at the central anode, using an iron screen to keep the two products physically separated so they cannot recombine.
elements: thick gray vessel wall (cross-section) with a flat top opening and bottom feed-throughs
molten NaCl bath filling the vessel, light blue/lavender fill, labeled 'Molten NaCl'
central anode (+): salmon/copper vertical rod with a flat top plate rising from the bottom center, labeled 'Anode (+)'
cylindrical iron screen: curved grid/mesh cage surrounding the anode, labeled 'Iron screen'
outer cathode (−): blue-gray vertical bars in the left and right annular region, labeled 'Cathode (−)'
central green-tinted collector tube rising from the anode zone, bending right at the top, with an upward arrow inside
green Cl2 gas bubbles/dots rising inside the collector tube
'Cl2 outlet' label with a rightward arrow at the top-right end of the green tube
'Inlet for NaCl' label with a small feed pipe at the top-right of the vessel
right-side collection reservoir (pinkish/lavender) holding liquid sodium, labeled 'Liquid Na metal'
'Na outlet' label with a rightward arrow draining from the bottom of the reservoir
gray 'Voltage source' box at the lower right
black connecting wires from the voltage source to the anode (bottom center) and to the cathode (right side)
migrating ion markers: Cl- ions (toward anode) and Na+ ions (toward cathode) shown during animation

interactions.label: Power the cell
interactions.teaches: Applying an external voltage is what forces the non-spontaneous decomposition of molten NaCl to proceed; with the power off the cell is just a static labeled apparatus.

interactions.label: Ion migration and product collection
interactions.teaches: Cl- ions drift inward to the central anode where they are oxidized to Cl2 gas that bubbles up and out the top outlet, while Na+ ions drift outward to the cathode where they are reduced to liquid Na that floats up and drains into the side reservoir.
Clicking an electrode isolates the half-reaction happening there: oxidation of chloride (2 Cl- -> Cl2 + 2 e-) at the anode and reduction of sodium ion (2 Na+ + 2 e- -> 2 Na) at the cathode.

demo_steps.title: The cell at rest
demo_steps.narration: With the power off, read the structure: a central anode caged by an iron screen, an outer cathode, a molten NaCl bath, and separate exit paths for gas (top) and liquid metal (side). Molten salt is used because in water the H+ would be reduced instead of Na+.

demo_steps.title: Run the electrolysis
demo_steps.narration: Powering the cell sets the ions in motion: Cl- migrates to the anode and leaves as rising Cl2 gas, Na+ migrates to the cathode and collects as liquid sodium. The iron screen keeps the two products apart so they cannot recombine.

demo_steps.title: Anode half-reaction
demo_steps.narration: Click the central anode to highlight it and reveal the oxidation half-equation 2 Cl- -> Cl2 + 2 e-, the source of the chlorine gas streaming out the top.

demo_steps.title: Cathode half-reaction
demo_steps.narration: Click the outer cathode to highlight it and reveal the reduction half-equation 2 Na+ + 2 e- -> 2 Na, the source of the liquid sodium draining from the side reservoir.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The Downs cell works because the iron screen physically separates the sodium and chlorine as they form, and because the salt is molten rather than aqueous so that Na+ — not water's H+ — is the species reduced at the cathode.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Cross-sectional layout: a thick gray rectangular vessel with an open top; molten NaCl as a flat light blue/lavender fill near the top. Center bottom: a salmon/copper anode rod with a flat cap, wrapped by a curved gray grid (iron screen). Outer left and right: short blue-gray cathode bars. From the anode zone a pale-green collector tube rises, narrows, then bends 90 degrees right at the top with an internal up-arrow and a 'Cl2 outlet' arrow; scatter small green dots inside it as gas. Top-right of vessel: a thin 'Inlet for NaCl' pipe. Right side: a pinkish bulb-shaped reservoir labeled 'Liquid Na metal' fed by a pipe from the cathode region, draining down to a 'Na outlet' arrow. Lower-right: a gray 'Voltage source' box wired in black to the anode base and the right cathode. During the animation, draw small labeled Cl- markers converging on the anode and Na+ markers moving outward to the cathode, with green bubbles rising and the reservoir level subtly filling. On click, outline the chosen electrode and show its balanced half-equation in a small callout near it. Keep all original text labels in their image positions.

authoredContext:
The most important method for the production of sodium is the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride; the set-up is a Downs cell , shown in . The reaction involved in this process is:

Separation of the molten sodium and chlorine prevents recombination. The liquid sodium, which is less dense than molten sodium chloride, floats to the surface and flows into a collector. The gaseous chlorine goes to storage tanks. Chlorine is also a valuable product.

Pure sodium metal is isolated by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride using a Downs cell. It is not possible to isolate sodium by electrolysis of aqueous solutions of sodium salts because hydrogen ions are more easily reduced than are sodium ions; as a result, hydrogen gas forms at the cathode instead of the desired sodium metal. The high temperature required to melt NaCl means that liquid sodium metal forms.

A diagram is shown. At the center of the diagram is a T-shaped structure labeled, “Anode ( positive sign ),” that is on a mesh-like background labeled, “Iron screen.” The anode is connected to a box labeled, “Voltage source,” by a line, and the voltage source is connected to one of two L-shaped structures that surround the anode. They are labeled, “Cathode ( negative sign ).” Above the cathode on the right side of the diagram is a tube connected to a collection chamber labeled, “N a metal,” that has a lower outlet labeled, “N a outlet.” Surrounding all of these components is a blue background labeled, “Molten N a C l,” and a series of tubes that form a square outside the diagram. They have an opening in the upper right corner labeled, “Inlet for N a C l.” At the top of the diagram is a large tube with an upward-facing arrow drawn on it. The tube turns right, has a right-facing arrow on it, and is labeled, “C l subscript 2 outlet.”

discrepancies: The right-hand 'Liquid Na metal' reservoir is drawn as a simple horizontal ellipse, whereas the source shows a taller vertical bulb/funnel vessel with a rounded top that tapers into a narrow drain neck.
The pale-green Cl₂ collector tube is a uniform-width stroke and lacks the flared trapezoidal widening at its base where it joins the top of the iron screen in the source.
The horizontal light-blue cathode current-collector bars that pass out through the left and right vessel walls in the source are absent; only the inner vertical cathode bars are drawn.
The iron screen is rendered as a smoothly rounded dome mesh rather than the more cylindrical vertical-grid cage with a flatter top seen in the source.
evaluation.notes: The Downs-cell layout, color scheme, and all major labels/leaders are faithfully reproduced and the power toggle, 4-step player, and click-to-reveal half-reactions are conceptually correct and functional, but the reservoir silhouette, the collector-tube base flare, and the external cathode collector bars deviate from the source geometry.
action_items: Redraw the right reservoir as the source's vertical bulb-with-funnel shape (rounded upper body tapering to a narrow neck into the drain pipe) instead of a plain ellipse, and reposition the 'Liquid Na metal' label/leader accordingly.
Add a flared trapezoidal base to the green Cl₂ collector tube where it meets the iron-screen dome to match the source funnel.
Add the horizontal blue cathode collector bars extending out through the left and right vessel walls, and route the cathode wire to one of them as in the source.
